Neonatal Common smooth-hounds (Mustelus mustelus) emerge from their mothers at a total length of approximately 36 centimeters [Lb = approximately 36 centimeters] at birth, a size that allows them to forage on small benthic crustaceans almost immediately after parturition. The gestation period in this species lasts roughly 438 days [ab = roughly 438 days], which, when examined under a consistent environmental temperature of 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C], appears to be a relatively prolonged developmental phase compared to some other triakid sharks. This extended gestation is thought to provide the developing pups with ample time for organogenesis and yolk absorption, ensuring they are well-prepared for independent life. The timing of birth likely coincides with periods of elevated prey abundance on the continental shelf, maximizing neonatal survival. Field surveys along the southern African coast have consistently documented neonates in shallow nursery grounds, where they benefit from reduced predation pressure and abundant food resources. The exact relationship between maternal body condition and the size of the pups at birth remains an active area of research, though preliminary data suggest that larger females may produce slightly longer neonates. Understanding the nuances of this early life stage is critical for constructing accurate demographic models for this commercially valuable species.

Males of Common smooth-hound attain sexual maturity at a significantly smaller body size compared to females, with puberty commencing around 98 centimeters [Lp = around 98 centimeters] in total length. This earlier maturation in males is a common pattern among elasmobranchs, likely driven by the reproductive advantages of achieving breeding status at a younger age, even at a smaller girth. By contrast, females do not typically reach puberty until they have grown to approximately 132 centimeters [Lp = approximately 132 centimeters] total length, a size disparity that reflects the greater energetic demands of gestation and the production of large, yolk-rich ova. These maturational thresholds are based on macroscopic inspection of gonadal tissue, revealing the onset of spermatogenesis in males and the development of mature ovarian follicles in females. The divergence in size at maturity between the sexes underscores a fundamental life-history trade-off: males prioritize early reproductive access, while females invest additional time in somatic growth to enhance their fecundity and offspring quality. Growth rates during the juvenile phase are consequently critical, as they determine the age at which individuals can first participate in the annual mating aggregations observed along the Agulhas Bank.

The ultimate total length achieved by this species shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females reaching a considerably larger maximum size than males. Females have been documented attaining an asymptotic body length of up to 204 centimeters [Li = up to 204 centimeters], whereas males typically cease growing at about 153 centimeters [Li = about 153 centimeters]. This size advantage in females is hypothesized to confer a direct reproductive benefit, as larger body cavities can accommodate a greater number of developing embryos. Corresponding to these length maxima, the ultimate wet weight of a full-grown female can reach approximately 29,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 29,100 grams], while a mature male rarely exceeds 11,900 grams [Wwi = 11,900 grams]. These mass estimates are derived from established length-weight conversion relationships and are consistent with specimens landed by commercial trawlers operating off the coast of Namibia. The markedly heavier female body mass reflects not only greater skeletal length but also the accumulation of substantial lipid reserves in the liver, which are vital for buoyancy control and energy storage during the lengthy reproductive cycle. Such pronounced sexual size dimorphism places Mustelus mustelus among the more extreme examples within its genus.

The reproductive output of the Common smooth-hound is characterized by a relatively low fecundity and a slow reproductive tempo, a strategy typical of many demersal sharks. Gravid females typically carry litters of approximately 20 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 20 pups per litter]. Furthermore, females produce only one litter every two years [F_R_i = one litter every two years], resulting in a modest annual reproductive rate. This leisurely reproductive schedule is tightly coupled to the thermal regime of their habitat; all observations on reproductive frequency have been conducted at a mean water temperature of 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C], conditions typical of the productive Benguela Current ecosystem. The combination of a small litter size and a biennial reproductive cycle means that population turnover is inherently slow, making the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing. Population viability analyses suggest that even moderate increases in adult mortality can lead to rapid declines, a concern that has prompted regional fisheries management measures. The long interval between successive pupping events necessitates a high rate of adult survival to maintain stable populations over time.

Maximum recorded longevity in the Common smooth-hound, based on vertebral band counts and tag-recapture studies, stands at approximately 24 years [am = approximately 24 years] for individuals maintained under the ambient oceanographic conditions of the southern Benguela, where the mean annual temperature is 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C]. This life span is comparable to that of other medium-sized triakid sharks and reflects a generally slow pace of life, with late maturity and low fecundity as key demographic correlates. The oldest individuals are typically large females that have successfully reproduced over many seasons, contributing disproportionately to the next generation. The combination of a long lifespan, high age at first reproduction, and low annual reproductive output places the Common smooth-hound firmly within the category of K-selected marine predators. Such life-history traits render the species highly susceptible to population depletion, as recovery times following exploitation are measured in decades rather than years. Ongoing monitoring programs continue to refine estimates of natural mortality and senescence, providing essential data for the sustainable management of this important fishery resource.
